adhikaram.english: Assertion of the Strength of Virtue

kurals.tamil:
சிறப்புஈனும் செல்வமும் ஈனும் அறத்தினூஉங்கு
ஆக்கம் எவனோ உயிர்க்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Sirappu eenum selvamum eenum araththinooungu,
Aakkam evano uyirkku.
kurals.meaning: Virtue yields honour and it yields prosperity too; so what greater good than virtue could there possibly be for any living being?
kurals.elementary: Imagine a tree that gives you both shade and fruit — you would not chop it down looking for something better. Doing the right thing is like that tree: it gives you a good name and it gives you good things in life, so there is nothing better to plant.
kurals.university: Valluvar opens the chapter with a rhetorical question rather than a command, staking out the claim that அறம் (aram, virtue/dharma) is not merely one good among many but the most productive of all. The pairing சிறப்பு (sirappu, 'distinction', glossed by the classical commentator Parimelazhagar as வீடுபேறு, liberation) with செல்வம் (selvam, wealth) collapses the usual opposition between otherworldly merit and worldly gain: virtue delivers both. This anticipates the tripartite scheme of aram–porul–inbam (dharma–artha–kama) that structures the Kural itself, and mirrors the classical Indian doctrine that dharma is the root from which artha and kama grow. The unusual archaic form அறத்தினூஉங்கு, with its alapedai (lengthened vowel), is metrically marked and gives the line its emphatic weight.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “With uplifted arms I am crying aloud but nobody hears me. From Righteousness is Wealth as also Pleasure. Why should not Righteousness, therefore, be courted?”
hinduism.explanation: This is Vyasa's despairing summary of the entire Mahabharata — the so-called Bharata Savitri — insisting that both material gain and enjoyment are downstream consequences of dharma, not rivals to it.
hinduism.tie_back: It makes exactly Valluvar's argument: since virtue is the source of both honour and wealth, nothing else can be a greater good.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata 18.5, Svargarohanika Parva (Bharata Savitri), trans. Kisari Mohan Ganguli
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: both texts assert that wealth and enjoyment flow from righteousness and then ask rhetorically why anything else would be pursued.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.”
christianity.explanation: In the Sermon on the Mount Jesus tells anxious listeners that food, drink and clothing follow on from putting righteousness first, rather than being secured by chasing them directly.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ranks righteousness above material gain precisely because material gain follows from it.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong structural match on 'virtue first, prosperity follows'; the Kural is non-theistic where Matthew is explicitly about God's kingdom.

islam.quote_or_event: “So be mindful of Allah to the best of your ability, hear and obey, and spend in charity—that will be best for you. And whoever is saved from the selfishness of their own souls, it is they who are ˹truly˺ successful.”
islam.explanation: The verse frames God-consciousness and generosity as what is genuinely 'best for you' (khayran li-anfusikum), redefining self-interest around righteous conduct.
islam.tie_back: Both texts argue that righteous conduct is the truly profitable course for a human being, not a sacrifice of profit.
islam.source: Qur'an 64:16, At-Taghabun (Dr. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)
islam._accuracy_note: Genuine overlap on 'piety is what is best for you', but the Qur'anic 'success' (falah) is eschatological, while Valluvar explicitly promises worldly wealth as well.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The following are the things for which a man enjoys the fruits in this world while the principal remains for him in the world to come: Honoring one’s father and mother; The performance of righteous deeds; And the making of peace between a person and his friend; And the study of the torah is equal to them all.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah classifies certain good deeds as paying a 'dividend' that can be enjoyed immediately while the capital is preserved for the world to come.
judaism.tie_back: It matches the Kural's double yield precisely: righteous action produces both present prosperity and ultimate distinction.
judaism.source: Mishnah Peah 1:1 (trans. Dr. Joshua Kulp, Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Unusually close — the this-world/next-world double return is the same structure Parimelazhagar reads into 'sirappu' and 'selvam'.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The doer of good rejoices here and hereafter; he rejoices in both the worlds. He rejoices and exults, recollecting his own pure deeds.”
buddhism.explanation: One of the Dhammapada's 'twin verses', contrasting the evil-doer who grieves in both worlds with the good-doer who rejoices in both.
buddhism.tie_back: Same claim that virtue pays out in this life and the next, leaving no greater good available to a living being.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close on the two-worlds benefit; the Dhammapada speaks of joy where the Kural speaks of honour and wealth.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “But they who give straight judgements to strangers and to the men of the land, and go not aside from what is just, their city flourishes, and the people prosper in it… The earth bears them victual in plenty… They flourish continually with good things.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod describes the city of the just as materially blessed by Zeus with peace, fertility and abundance, in direct contrast to the famine and ruin visited on the unjust city.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's claim in mythic-agricultural form: righteousness itself is what generates prosperity.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 225-237, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong on 'justice produces prosperity'; Hesiod's mechanism is divine reward for a community, whereas Valluvar's is an impersonal claim about individual life.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “I tell you that virtue is not given by money, but that from virtue come money and every other good of man, public as well as private.”
philosophy.explanation: At his trial Socrates defends his life's work of urging Athenians to care for the soul before possessions, claiming that goods flow from virtue rather than the reverse.
philosophy.tie_back: This is almost a direct Greek restatement of Kural 31: virtue is the source of wealth and every other good, so nothing exceeds it.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Exceptionally tight parallel — both explicitly reverse the assumed causality between wealth and virtue.

adhikaram.english: Assertion of the Strength of Virtue

kurals.tamil:
அறத்தினூஉங்கு ஆக்கமும் இல்லை அதனை
மறத்தலின் ஊங்கில்லை கேடு.
kurals.transliteration:
Araththinooungu aakkamum illai adhanai,
Maraththalin oongillai kedu.
kurals.meaning: There is no greater gain than virtue, and there is no greater ruin than forgetting it.
kurals.elementary: Think of brushing your teeth. Doing it is the best thing for your teeth, and forgetting to do it is the worst thing for them. This kural says goodness works the same way — doing it is the best thing possible, and forgetting about it is the worst.
kurals.university: The couplet is built on a deliberate chiasmus: ஆக்கம் (aakkam, increase/gain) is set against கேடு (kedu, ruin/loss), and the pivot between them is not 'doing evil' but மறத்தல் (marathal, forgetting). Valluvar's diagnosis of moral failure is therefore cognitive rather than volitional — Parimelazhagar glosses the forgetting as arising from மயக்கம் (delusion), not defiance. This makes the verse subtly different from ordinary two-path moralism: the opposite of virtue is not vice but inattention. The verse also repeats அறத்தினூஉங்கு from Kural 31, a rhetorical device (antadi-like linkage) binding the chapter's opening pair into a single argument.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Justice, being violated, destroys; justice, being preserved, preserves: therefore justice must not be violated, lest violated justice destroy us.”
hinduism.explanation: The Sanskrit maxim dharmo rakṣati rakṣitaḥ presents dharma as reciprocal: it guards whoever guards it and destroys whoever abandons it.
hinduism.tie_back: It states the Kural's exact two-sidedness — maximum gain from upholding virtue, maximum ruin from letting it go.
hinduism.source: Manusmriti 8.15, trans. Georg Bühler (Sacred Books of the East, 1886)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Almost a perfect structural twin; Manu frames it as active violation where Valluvar frames it as forgetting.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus sets total worldly acquisition against the loss of one's own self, arguing that no quantity of gain compensates for that loss.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it measures gain and ruin on a single scale and concludes that moral loss is the greatest possible ruin.
christianity._accuracy_note: Captures the 'no greater loss' half very well; the 'no greater gain than virtue' half is implied rather than stated.

islam.quote_or_event: “Successful indeed is the one who purifies their soul, and doomed is the one who corrupts it!”
islam.explanation: The closing oath-sequence of Surah Ash-Shams distils all human outcomes into a single antithesis between purifying (zakkāhā) and corrupting (dassāhā) the soul.
islam.tie_back: Both couplets reduce human fortune to one binary: maintaining moral integrity is the whole of gain, abandoning it the whole of ruin.
islam.source: Qur'an 91:9-10, Ash-Shams (Dr. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)
islam._accuracy_note: Very strong parallel in form and content; 'success/doom' maps cleanly onto aakkam/kedu.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I call heaven and earth to witness against you this day: I have put before you life and death, blessing and curse. Choose life—if you and your offspring would live—”
judaism.explanation: Moses' closing charge presents obedience to the covenant not as one option among many but as the choice between existence and annihilation.
judaism.tie_back: It gives the same stark two-sided accounting the Kural does: righteousness is all gain, its abandonment all ruin.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong on the binary structure; Deuteronomy's frame is covenantal and national, the Kural's is individual and universal.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Should a person commit evil, let him not do it again and again. Let him not find pleasure therein, for painful is the accumulation of evil. Should a person do good, let him do it again and again. Let him find pleasure therein, for blissful is the accumulation of good.”
buddhism.explanation: This paired verse presents merit and demerit as accumulating stocks whose eventual ripening is guaranteed, pleasant in one case and painful in the other.
buddhism.tie_back: Same symmetrical ledger as the Kural: the accumulation of good is the greatest gain, its opposite the greatest loss.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close on the gain/ruin symmetry, though the Dhammapada emphasises repetition rather than the Kural's 'forgetting'.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aeschylus' Eumenides the Furies, ancient goddesses of blood-vengeance, argue before the Athenian court that if Orestes goes unpunished every restraint on human wrongdoing will dissolve, and they warn the city that there are times when dread must sit enthroned over the heart, since neither anarchy nor tyranny follows where reverence is kept.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Furies are making a civic argument: the forgetting of retributive justice is not a local error but the collapse of the moral order that holds a society together.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It dramatises the Kural's second line — the forgetting of dharma is itself the supreme catastrophe.
greek_mythology.source: Aeschylus, Eumenides, the Furies' choral ode (ll. 490-565)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Thematically apt on 'forgetting justice equals ruin', but Aeschylus is arguing about institutional punishment, not about personal virtue as the highest gain.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Republic Book IV Socrates concludes that justice is the health, beauty and good condition of the soul while injustice is its disease, deformity and weakness — so that asking whether injustice pays is as absurd as asking whether it pays to have a ruined body.
philosophy.explanation: The argument makes moral condition intrinsic rather than instrumental: virtue is what the soul's flourishing consists of, and vice is its destruction.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's claim rendered as an argument: nothing can outweigh virtue as gain, and nothing can rival its loss as ruin.
philosophy._accuracy_note: The health/disease analogy reproduces the Kural's two-sided maximum claim closely; paraphrased rather than quoted because translations vary widely.

adhikaram.english: Assertion of the Strength of Virtue

kurals.tamil:
ஒல்லும் வகையான் அறவினை ஓவாதே
செல்லும்வாய் எல்லாஞ் செயல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ollum vakaiyaan aravinai ovaadhe,
Sellumvaai ellaanj cheyal.
kurals.meaning: By whatever means you are able, without ever letting up, do good in every situation where good can be done.
kurals.elementary: You do not need to be strong to help. If you can carry one book, carry one book. This kural says: do whatever good you can manage, wherever you happen to be, and do not stop.
kurals.university: Three qualifiers do the work here. ஒல்லும் வகையான் ('by the means available to you') scales the obligation to individual capacity — Parimelazhagar specifies that the householder gives according to his means and the ascetic according to his bodily strength. ஓவாதே ('without ceasing') removes any notion of virtue as an occasional act. செல்லும்வாய் எல்லாம् ('in every place it can reach') is glossed by the commentators as the three instruments of mind, speech and body (மனம், வாக்கு, காயம்), yielding good thought, good word and good deed. The verse thus converts virtue from a discrete achievement into a continuous disposition, and does so without ever specifying a quantity — a characteristically Tamil ethical move that keeps the demand universal and the standard personal.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Therefore, without being attached to the fruits of activities, one should act as a matter of duty, for by working without attachment one attains the Supreme.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna's central instruction in the karma-yoga chapter is that right action is to be performed constantly (satatam) as duty, without calculating its returns.
hinduism.tie_back: Both verses make virtuous action a continuous obligation rather than an occasional or result-driven one.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.19 (Bhaktivedanta, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong on constancy of right action; the Gita adds non-attachment to fruits, which the Kural does not raise here.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not. As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith.”
christianity.explanation: Paul urges the Galatians to sustained rather than sporadic good-doing, and to take every opportunity as it arises.
christianity.tie_back: It reproduces all three of the Kural's qualifiers — as you are able, without slackening, wherever the chance arises.
christianity._accuracy_note: One of the closest matches in the chapter: 'not weary' = ஓவாதே, 'as we have opportunity' = ஒல்லும் வகையான், 'unto all men' = செல்லும்வாய் எல்லாம்.

islam.quote_or_event: “So be mindful of Allah to the best of your ability, hear and obey, and spend in charity—that will be best for you.”
islam.explanation: The phrase mā istaṭa'tum — 'to the extent you are able' — is the Qur'an's standard scaling of religious obligation to individual capacity.
islam.tie_back: It is the Qur'anic equivalent of ஒல்லும் வகையான்: do the good that lies within your power, whatever that power happens to be.
islam.source: Qur'an 64:16, At-Taghabun (Dr. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)
islam._accuracy_note: Direct match on the capacity clause; the 'without ceasing' element is present only implicitly.

judaism.quote_or_event: “It is not your duty to finish the work, but neither are you at liberty to neglect it.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Tarfon's maxim releases a person from the impossible demand of completing the moral task while forbidding them to opt out of it.
judaism.tie_back: It captures the Kural's balance exactly: do what you are capable of, but never stop doing it.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 2:16 (trans. Dr. Joshua Kulp, Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Very strong on the capacity/continuity pairing; Avot's framing is about Torah study and communal work rather than good deeds generally.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Hasten to do good; restrain your mind from evil. He who is slow in doing good, his mind delights in evil.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada treats slowness in doing good not as neutral but as actively dangerous, since the unoccupied mind drifts toward harm.
buddhism.tie_back: It sharpens the Kural's ஓவாதே: there is no safe pause in the practice of virtue.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close on urgency and continuity; the Dhammapada lacks the Kural's 'according to your means' qualification.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Heracles, to expiate his crime, is set twelve labours by Eurystheus and must complete every one of them; when two are disallowed on technicalities he is made to perform substitutes, and only after the whole sequence is finished without exception does he earn release and, ultimately, immortality.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth makes the point that the labours cannot be partially discharged — the reward attaches to the unbroken completion of the whole series, in whatever terrain and by whatever means each demands.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It offers a mythic image of the Kural's 'ceaselessly, by every means, wherever the work can be done'.
greek_mythology.source: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5 (the Twelve Labours of Heracles)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Honest stretch: the labours are penance under compulsion, not freely chosen everyday virtue — the shared element is only unremitting, adaptive effort.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For the things we have to learn before we can do them, we learn by doing them, e.g. men become builders by building and lyreplayers by playing the lyre; so too we become just by doing just acts, temperate by doing temperate acts, brave by doing brave acts.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle's doctrine of habituation holds that moral character is not taught but built up through the repeated performance of the corresponding actions.
philosophy.tie_back: It supplies the reason behind the Kural's insistence on unceasing practice: virtue exists only as sustained activity.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.1 (1103a-b), trans. W. D. Ross
philosophy._accuracy_note: Excellent philosophical underpinning for the Kural's 'without ceasing'; Aristotle is explaining character formation rather than commanding action.

adhikaram.english: Assertion of the Strength of Virtue

kurals.tamil:
மனத்துக்கண் மாசிலன் ஆதல் அனைத்தறன்
ஆகுல நீர பிற.
kurals.transliteration:
Manaththukkan maasilan aadhal anaiththu aran,
Aakula neera pira.
kurals.meaning: To be free of stain in the mind — that alone is virtue; everything else is mere noise and display.
kurals.elementary: You can wash the outside of a cup and still leave it dirty inside, and nobody would want to drink from it. This kural says goodness is about being clean on the inside; showing off on the outside is just noise.
kurals.university: This is one of the Kural's most radical reductions: அனைத்து அறன் — 'that is the whole of virtue' — locates morality entirely in மனத்துக்கண் மாசு, stain in the mind. The dismissive ஆகுல நீர ('of the nature of clamour') is aimed, on Manakkudavar's reading, at conduct performed so that others will notice it; Parimelazhagar extends it to outward religious garb (வேடம்) and pious talk. Coming immediately after a verse commanding ceaseless outward action, Kural 34 prevents that command from collapsing into ritualism, and it prepares the ground for Kural 35's inventory of specifically mental vices. The move parallels — but does not derive from — the Jain and Buddhist emphasis on cetanā (intention) as the locus of karma, and is one reason the Kural has been read as compatible with renunciant and householder ethics alike.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “And satisfaction, simplicity, gravity, self-control and purification of one’s existence are the austerities of the mind.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna distinguishes austerities of body, speech and mind, and defines mental austerity as inner purification rather than any visible act.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats purity of mind as a discipline in its own right, distinct from and more fundamental than outward observance.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 17.16 (Bhaktivedanta, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong on the primacy of mental purity; the Gita still retains bodily and verbal austerities as valid, where the Kural dismisses the rest as show.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Take heed that ye do not your alms before men, to be seen of them: otherwise ye have no reward of your Father which is in heaven.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that charitable acts performed for an audience have already received their entire payment in the applause they collect.
christianity.tie_back: This is precisely the Kural's ஆகுல நீர — outward virtue done to be seen is clamour, not virtue.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close on the critique of performative virtue; Matthew's criterion is divine reward rather than the Kural's inner stainlessness.

islam.quote_or_event: “The reward of deeds depends upon the intentions and every person will get the reward according to what he has intended.”
islam.explanation: The opening hadith of Sahih al-Bukhari — innamā al-a'mālu bi'l-niyyāt — makes inward intention the thing that determines the moral value of any outward act.
islam.tie_back: It states the Kural's thesis in legal form: the mind's condition is the whole of the act's worth.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 1, narrated by 'Umar ibn al-Khattab
islam._accuracy_note: Outstanding match — this hadith is the canonical Islamic statement that inner state, not outward deed, constitutes moral reality.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Pay no attention to his appearance or his stature, for I have rejected him. For [God sees] not as humans see; humans see only what is visible, but God sees into the heart.”
judaism.explanation: God rebukes Samuel for judging Saul's successor by outward impressiveness, and directs him instead to David on the basis of what is inward.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts insist that the real seat of worth is the heart, and that visible impressiveness proves nothing.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong on inner-versus-outer; the verse is about divine evaluation of a person rather than a definition of virtue as such.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Mind precedes all mental states. Mind is their chief; they are all mind-wrought. If with an impure mind a person speaks or acts suffering follows him like the wheel that follows the foot of the ox.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada's opening verse makes mind the origin of all conduct, so that the moral quality of speech and action is entirely derivative of the mind's condition.
buddhism.tie_back: It grounds the Kural's claim: if all action is mind-wrought, then freedom from stain in the mind really is the whole of virtue.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close — both verses make the mind the exclusive seat of moral quality and treat outward acts as downstream.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Herodotus tells of Glaucus the Spartan, famed for honesty, who was entrusted with another man's money and later considered keeping it. He asked the Delphic oracle whether he might swear an oath and retain the deposit, and the Pythia replied that merely to have tempted the god with such a question was as fatal as the perjury itself; Glaucus returned the money, but his family line was wiped out regardless.
greek_mythology.explanation: The story makes the intention alone — never acted upon, and immediately renounced — fully sufficient for ruin, because the stain was already in the mind.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It dramatises the Kural's claim that moral reality is located in the mind's condition, not in the outward deed.
greek_mythology.source: Herodotus, Histories 6.86 (the story of Glaucus of Sparta)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Thematically excellent on inner stain, but it comes from a historian's oracle-tale rather than myth proper, and its logic is punitive where the Kural's is definitional.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Nothing can possibly be conceived in the world, or even out of it, which can be called good, without qualification, except a good will.”
philosophy.explanation: Kant opens the Groundwork by arguing that talents, temperament and even happiness can all be turned to harm, so that the only unconditionally good thing is the will's inner orientation.
philosophy.tie_back: It is Kural 34 as a philosophical thesis: moral worth resides wholly in the inner disposition, and nothing outward qualifies without it.
philosophy.source: Immanuel Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysic of Morals, opening of Section I, trans. Thomas Kingsmill Abbott
philosophy._accuracy_note: Remarkably close in claim and in exclusivity ('nothing... except' mirrors 'அனைத்து அறன்'), though Kant is arguing from autonomy and Valluvar from purity.

adhikaram.english: Assertion of the Strength of Virtue

kurals.tamil:
அழுக்காறு அவாவெகுளி இன்னாச்சொல் நான்கும்
இழுக்கா இயன்றது அறம்.
kurals.transliteration:
Azhukkaaru avaavekuli innaachchol naankum,
Izhukkaa iyandradhu aram.
kurals.meaning: Conduct that keeps clear of all four — envy, greed, anger and harsh speech — and goes on steadily: that is virtue.
kurals.elementary: Four things spoil a good day: wanting what your friend has, wanting more and more for yourself, losing your temper, and saying something mean. This kural says being good mostly means steering around those four.
kurals.university: Valluvar here gives virtue a negative definition — a via negativa built from four named faults, each of which will later receive its own chapter or sub-treatment in the Kural. அழுக்காறு (envy at another's prosperity), அவா (craving running out through the senses), வெகுளி (the anger that erupts when craving is blocked) and இன்னாச்சொல் (the harsh word that anger produces) are arranged by Parimelazhagar as a causal chain rather than a list, so the four are really one process caught at four stages. The verbal form இழுக்கா ('not slipping') is a negative participle drawn from the vocabulary of footing and balance, so the image is of walking a path without stumbling. Note the textual crux: some manuscripts and a persistent popular tradition read ஈயாமை (miserliness) in place of நான்கும், but the reading with நான்கும் is the one carried by the major commentarial tradition and by the standard printed editions used here.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “There are three gates leading to this hell – lust, anger and greed. Every sane man should give these up, for they lead to the degradation of the soul.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names kāma, krodha and lobha as the three entrances to ruin, and makes their abandonment the precondition of any genuine spiritual progress.
hinduism.tie_back: Three of Valluvar's four faults appear here as a named set to be renounced, defining right conduct by exclusion just as the Kural does.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 16.21 (Bhaktivedanta, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong overlap on craving, anger and greed; the Gita's list omits envy and harsh speech, and Valluvar's 'avā' covers both lust and greed.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice:”
christianity.explanation: Paul lists the interior dispositions and their verbal outlets together, treating the malice behind the words and the words themselves as one package to be discarded.
christianity.tie_back: It matches the Kural's structure of defining virtue as steady conduct cleared of a short, named list of faults.
christianity._accuracy_note: Covers anger, harsh speech and malice precisely; greed is absent from this particular verse.

islam.quote_or_event: In a hadith recorded by Muslim, the Prophet forbids a cluster of interpersonal faults in a single breath — envying one another, driving up prices against one another, hating one another, turning away from one another, undercutting one another's sales — commands believers to live as brothers, and then strikes his own chest three times saying that piety (taqwa) is here.
islam.explanation: The list works exactly like a definition by exclusion, and the gesture toward the chest relocates piety from the listed outward behaviours to the heart that produces them.
islam.tie_back: It gives virtue the same shape the Kural does: a named set of interpersonal faults avoided, with the real seat of the matter in the heart.
islam.source: Sahih Muslim 2564a, narrated by Abu Hurayra
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrased rather than quoted because the standard English rendering on Sunnah.com is unidiomatic; envy and hatred match well, greed and harsh speech only partially.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Elazar Ha-kappar said: envy, lust and [the desire for] honor put a man out of the world.”
judaism.explanation: A compact rabbinic maxim naming three appetites that destroy a person's standing in this world and the next.
judaism.tie_back: It is the same rhetorical move as the Kural — a short enumerated list of faults whose avoidance constitutes a whole ethic.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 4:21 (trans. Dr. Joshua Kulp, Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Envy and craving match exactly and the list-form is identical; honour-seeking replaces the Kural's anger and harsh speech.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Saleyyaka Sutta the Buddha itemises the ten courses of unwholesome action for the brahmins of Sala, and among them are harsh speech — words that are rough, bitter and abusive to others — covetousness for what belongs to another, and a mind of ill will; conduct in accordance with the Dhamma is then defined simply as the abstention from each of these.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta's whole method is to define right conduct as the negation of an enumerated list of bodily, verbal and mental faults.
buddhism.tie_back: Three of the Kural's four faults appear in that list, and the definitional method — virtue as what remains when the named faults are excluded — is identical.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 41, Saleyyaka Sutta (the ten courses of unwholesome and wholesome action)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Method and content align closely; paraphrased because the sutta's list is long and no single sentence quotes cleanly.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid's Metamorphoses Athena, angered by the jealous Aglauros, sends her to the house of Invidia (Envy) — a black, rotting dwelling where the goddess sits gnawing vipers, never smiling, wasting away at the sight of others' good fortune. Invidia breathes her poison into Aglauros' breast, and the girl is consumed from within until she hardens into black stone on the threshold she had jealously guarded.
greek_mythology.explanation: Envy is portrayed as a self-destroying corrosion that literally petrifies the person who hosts it, rather than as an injury done to its object.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It gives vivid mythic form to the first item in the Kural's list of four, and to the idea that these faults ruin the person who harbours them.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Powerful on envy alone; it does not address greed, anger or harsh speech, and offers no definition of virtue, so it is a partial match.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But not every action nor every passion admits of a mean; for some have names that already imply badness, e.g. spite, shamelessness, envy, and in the case of actions adultery, theft, murder… It is not possible, then, ever to be right with regard to them; one must always be wrong.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle carves out an exception to his own doctrine of the mean: certain named passions and acts are bad in themselves, admitting no correct amount or occasion.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural's four, these are faults to be excluded outright rather than moderated, and virtue is what proceeds without slipping into them.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.6 (1107a), trans. W. D. Ross
philosophy._accuracy_note: Envy appears by name and the 'always wrong, never moderated' logic matches the Kural's absolute exclusion; Aristotle's list differs in its other items.

adhikaram.english: Assertion of the Strength of Virtue

kurals.tamil:
அன்றறிவாம் என்னாது அறஞ்செய்க மற்றது
பொன்றுங்கால் பொன்றாத் துணை.
kurals.transliteration:
Andrarivaam ennaadhu aranjeyka matradhu,
Pondrungaal pondraath thunai.
kurals.meaning: Do not say 'we will see to it when the time comes' — do good now; for when you perish, that alone will be the companion that does not perish.
kurals.elementary: If you keep saying you will pack your bag tomorrow, one day the bus leaves without you. This kural says do good things today, because they are the only things that stay with you when everything else is gone.
kurals.university: The idiom அன்றறிவாம் — literally 'we shall know on that day' — is the voice of procrastination personified; Parimelazhagar expands it as the young person's reasoning, 'we are young now, we will do it at the hour of death.' Against this Valluvar sets the wordplay that gives the couplet its force: பொன்றுங்கால் பொன்றாத் துணை, 'at the time of perishing, the unperishing companion', built on repetition of the root பொன்று- in opposite senses. The image of virtue as துணை (companion, escort) that accompanies the soul past the body's dissolution is shared with Jain and Buddhist merit-doctrine, and Manakkudavar reads it explicitly as support in the next birth; the Dravidian rationalist commentator Kalaignar Karunanidhi instead reads it as imperishable fame. The verse is one of the clearest places where the Kural's deliberate theological reticence allows two very different readings of the same line.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The Supreme Personality of Godhead said: Son of Pṛthā, a transcendentalist engaged in auspicious activities does not meet with destruction either in this world or in the spiritual world; one who does good, My friend, is never overcome by evil.”
hinduism.explanation: Answering Arjuna's fear that an unfinished spiritual effort is simply wasted, Krishna assures him that accumulated good is never destroyed and carries across the break of death.
hinduism.tie_back: It is the Kural's promise in reverse: because good done is indestructible, there is no reason to defer it and every reason to begin.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 6.40 (Bhaktivedanta, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very strong on virtue surviving death as an imperishable asset; the Gita does not include the Kural's rebuke of procrastination.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And I heard a voice from heaven saying unto me, Write, Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth: Yea, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours; and their works do follow them.”
christianity.explanation: The vision declares that a person's deeds accompany them past death — the labours cease but the works travel on with the doer.
christianity.tie_back: 'Their works do follow them' is almost a translation of பொன்றுங்கால் பொன்றாத் துணை, the companion that does not perish.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near-exact on the second line's image; the first line's 'do not defer' has no counterpart in this verse.

islam.quote_or_event: “When a man dies, his acts come to an end, but three, recurring charity, or knowledge (by which people) benefit, or a pious child, who prays for him (for the deceased).”
islam.explanation: The hadith of ṣadaqa jāriya identifies the specific forms of good whose benefit continues to accrue to a person after the account of their deeds has otherwise closed.
islam.tie_back: It names exactly what the Kural means by the unperishing companion — the good done in life that outlives the doer.
islam.source: Sahih Muslim 1631, narrated by Abu Hurayra
islam._accuracy_note: Outstanding match on the imperishable-companion image; the urgency of 'do not postpone' is implicit in the hadith rather than stated.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Eliezer said: Let the honor of your friend be as dear to you as your own; And be not easily provoked to anger; And repent one day before your death.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud records that Rabbi Eliezer's students objected that no one knows the day of their death, to which he answered: all the more reason, then, to repent today — lest one die tomorrow.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's first line almost word for word: do not tell yourself you will attend to it when the time comes.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 2:10 (trans. Dr. Joshua Kulp, Sefaria); cf. b. Shabbat 153a
judaism._accuracy_note: Exceptional match on the anti-procrastination argument; Avot speaks of repentance where the Kural speaks of doing good.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “As kinsmen welcome a dear one on arrival, even so his own good deeds will welcome the doer of good who has gone from this world to the next.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada pictures a person's accumulated merit waiting for them on the far side of death like family gathered to greet a returning traveller.
buddhism.tie_back: It is the Kural's 'companion that does not perish', rendered as a homecoming rather than an escort.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Among the closest matches in this chapter — same claim, same crossing-of-death frame, same warmth of the companionship image.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Do not put your work off till to-morrow and the day after; for a sluggish worker does not fill his barn, nor one who puts off his work: industry makes work go well, but a man who puts off work is always at hand-grips with ruin.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod's farming advice to his brother Perses treats deferral itself as the decisive cause of poverty and disaster, independent of ability or circumstance.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the Kural's first line transposed to the farm — the one who says 'later' is already losing.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 410-413, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Very close on procrastination but Hesiod is talking about agricultural labour, not virtue, and has nothing corresponding to the companion beyond death.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “While we are postponing, life speeds by.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca opens his first letter to Lucilius by urging him to gather and hold his time, since time is the only thing truly ours and the only loss that cannot be made good.
philosophy.tie_back: It supplies the reason the Kural forbids 'we shall know on that day': the day one is reserving for virtue is being spent right now.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 1 (On Saving Time), trans. Richard M. Gummere
philosophy._accuracy_note: Sharp match on the anti-deferral argument; Seneca is concerned with time as such rather than specifically with moral action.

adhikaram.english: Assertion of the Strength of Virtue

kurals.tamil:
அறத்தாறு இதுவென வேண்டா சிவிகை
பொறுத்தானோடு ஊர்ந்தான் இடை.
kurals.transliteration:
Araththaaru ithuvena ventaa sivikai,
Poruththaanotu oorndhaan itai.
kurals.meaning: There is no need for anyone to expound what the fruit of virtue is: just look at the difference between the man carrying the palanquin and the man riding in it.
kurals.elementary: Some things you do not need explained — you just look. Two people are on the same road: one is carrying the chair, one is sitting in it. This kural says the difference between doing good and not doing good shows up like that, plain to see.
kurals.university: This is the Kural's most striking piece of epistemology. Parimelazhagar reads the verse in the technical vocabulary of Indian logic: there is no need for ஆகம அளவை (scriptural testimony, verbal authority) because காட்சி அளவை (pratyakṣa, direct perception) settles the matter. Valluvar is arguing that karmic consequence is empirically visible in the unequal fortunes of the palanquin-bearer and the palanquin-rider, an argument for virtue that requires no revelation. The verse has also been the chapter's most contested: modern readers, including Kalaignar Karunanidhi in his widely read commentary, have resisted the implication that social inequality is morally deserved, and reinterpret the pair as contrasting inner ease with inner burden rather than birth-station. Either way the rhetorical claim stands — the strength of virtue is a matter of observation, not argument.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Among them, those who did good work in this world [in their past life] attain a good birth accordingly. They are born as a brāhmin, a kṣatriya, or a vaiśya. But those who did bad work in this world [in their past life] attain a bad birth accordingly, being born as a dog, a pig, or as a casteless person.”
hinduism.explanation: The Chandogya's teaching of the two paths explains the visible inequality of births as the direct ripening of conduct in a previous life.
hinduism.tie_back: It supplies precisely the doctrine that makes the Kural's palanquin image legible — present station reads off past conduct.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close doctrinally; both texts are also open to the same modern objection that they naturalise social hierarchy.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Ye shall know them by their fruits. Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles? Even so every good tree bringeth forth good fruit; but a corrupt tree bringeth forth evil fruit.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus offers an empirical test for distinguishing true teachers from false: do not weigh their claims, observe what their lives produce.
christianity.tie_back: Same epistemic move as the Kural — do not expound the fruit of virtue in words, point at what is visible.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong on 'judge by observable results rather than testimony'; the content of the fruit differs, and there is no rebirth dimension.

islam.quote_or_event: “They will each be assigned ranks according to their deeds. And your Lord is not unaware of what they do.”
islam.explanation: The verse establishes that differences of rank (darajāt) among created beings correspond exactly to what each has done.
islam.tie_back: It gives the Kural's contrast its principle: the gap between bearer and rider is a difference of rank proportioned to deeds.
islam.source: Qur'an 6:132, Al-An'am (Dr. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on deeds determining rank; in Islam the decisive ranking is at the Judgement rather than visibly in this life, which weakens the empirical parallel.

judaism.quote_or_event: “With the measure that a person measures, he is measured with it.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah states the principle of middah k'neged middah, measure for measure, and then reads a series of visible outcomes as exactly proportioned to the conduct that produced them.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts read observable difference in fortune as a legible record of prior conduct.
judaism._accuracy_note: The proportionality principle matches well, but the Mishnah applies it within a single lifetime and to a specific ritual case, not across births.

buddhism.quote_or_event: King Ajatasattu asks the Buddha whether there is any fruit of the contemplative life that can actually be seen here and now, in the way a trainer of elephants or a cook can point to the visible benefit of his craft. The Buddha answers by asking the king what he would do if his own slave were to go forth and live virtuously — would he order him back to servitude? The king admits he would rise and offer him a seat; and the Buddha says: that is a fruit of the contemplative life, visible here and now.
buddhism.explanation: The whole sutta is constructed around the demand for sandiṭṭhika — a result that can be pointed at rather than merely asserted — and the Buddha meets it with an everyday social observation.
buddhism.tie_back: It is the Kural's argument staged as a dialogue, complete with a contrast between the man who serves and the man who is served.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 2, Samaññaphala Sutta (The Fruits of the Contemplative Life)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strikingly parallel in method and even in imagery; paraphrased because the exchange runs over several pages with no single quotable sentence.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Jupiter and Mercury, disguised as travellers, are turned away from a thousand doors in Phrygia until the poor old couple Baucis and Philemon take them in and share what little they have. The gods lead them up the hillside, and from there the couple watch the whole inhospitable district sink beneath a marsh while their own cottage is transformed into a gleaming temple.
greek_mythology.explanation: The reward and the ruin are made simultaneously visible from one vantage point, so the moral difference between the couple and their neighbours becomes a difference anyone can see in the landscape.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's roadside scene, it asks the observer simply to look at two conditions side by side and read the fruit of virtue off them.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Shares the 'look and compare' structure, but the outcome is direct divine intervention rather than the impersonal ripening of deeds the Kural implies.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Republic Book IX Socrates sets the just and the tyrannical lives side by side and argues that anyone who could see inside the tyrant would find the least free and most wretched of men, despite his apparent mastery — and he invites Glaucon to judge the ranking of lives by inspection rather than by argument.
philosophy.explanation: The argument turns on the claim that the true condition of a life is discoverable by looking at it whole, and that appearances of mastery and servitude can be exactly inverted.
philosophy.tie_back: It is the same comparative method as the Kural's palanquin, with the added twist that the one who appears to ride may be the one who is carried.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good on the side-by-side comparative method; Plato's point inverts outward appearances where Valluvar takes them at face value.

adhikaram.english: Assertion of the Strength of Virtue

kurals.tamil:
வீழ்நாள் படாஅமை நன்றாற்றின் அஃதொருவன்
வாழ்நாள் வழியடைக்கும் கல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Veezhnaal pataaamai nandraatrin aqdhoruvan,
Vaazhnaal vazhiyataikkum kal.
kurals.meaning: If a person does good without letting a single day fall away empty, that practice becomes the stone that blocks the road by which further births would come.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a gate that keeps swinging open, and every day you do a good thing you push a stone a little closer to it. Do it every single day and eventually the stone sits right in the gateway and the gate cannot open again.
kurals.university: The couplet turns on two metaphors that must be held together. வீழ்நாள் — a 'fallen day', a day let slip without good done — is set against கல், a blocking stone. Parimelazhagar reads வாழ்நாள் வழி as the road by which embodied life keeps recurring, so the daily practice of aram literally walls up the passage of rebirth; he glosses the whole verse as the statement that virtue yields வீடு (liberation), and imports the five kleśas of the Sanskrit tradition to explain what keeps the road open. The image of blocking rather than escaping is unusual and concrete — the Kural does not speak of transcending the cycle but of obstructing it, as one blocks a cattle-track with a boulder. Modern rationalist commentators such as Kalaignar Karunanidhi, resisting the rebirth reading, take கல் instead as a paving-stone that smooths the road of one's own life.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “By thus engaging in devotional service to the Lord, great sages or devotees free themselves from the results of work in the material world. In this way they become free from the cycle of birth and death and attain the state beyond all miseries.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes janma-bandha-vinirmukta — release from the bondage of birth — as the outcome of sustained right practice.
hinduism.tie_back: It names exactly what the Kural's stone accomplishes: the closing of the road by which birth recurs.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.51 (Bhaktivedanta, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong on the rebirth-ending outcome; the Gita's means is devotional service rather than the Kural's daily unbroken good works.

christianity.quote_or_event: “See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise, Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.”
christianity.explanation: Paul urges the Ephesians to buy back their days from waste, treating each day as something that can be lost or reclaimed.
christianity.tie_back: It matches the Kural's first line — let no day fall away — though Christianity has no equivalent for blocking rebirth.
christianity._accuracy_note: Honest partial match: good on daily non-wastage, but the entire second half of the Kural, about obstructing the path of further births, has no Christian counterpart.

islam.quote_or_event: “Do good deeds properly, sincerely and moderately and know that your deeds will not make you enter Paradise, and that the most beloved deed to Allah is the most regular and constant even if it were little.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet commends sustained daily practice over intense but intermittent effort, explicitly valuing regularity above magnitude.
islam.tie_back: It is the Kural's 'let no day fall away' stated as a rule of spiritual method: small and daily beats large and occasional.
islam._accuracy_note: Excellent on daily constancy; Islam's linear eschatology means the rebirth-blocking half has no parallel.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Tarfon said: the day is short, and the work is plentiful, and the laborers are indolent, and the reward is great, and the master of the house is insistent.”
judaism.explanation: The saying presses the urgency of each day against the size of the moral task, treating any idle day as a real and irrecoverable loss.
judaism.tie_back: It captures the Kural's insistence that a day without good done is a day that has fallen.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 2:15 (trans. Dr. Joshua Kulp, Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Good on daily urgency; mainstream Judaism has no rebirth doctrine to match the Kural's second line, so this is a deliberate half-match.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “O house-builder, you are seen! You will not build this house again. For your rafters are broken and your ridgepole shattered. My mind has reached the Unconditioned; I have attained the destruction of craving.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha's verse of victory addresses craving as the builder who has repeatedly constructed the house of embodied existence, and declares that it will never build again.
buddhism.tie_back: It is the Kural's image in construction rather than obstruction: the mechanism of repeated birth is permanently disabled.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very strong on the rebirth-ending image; the Buddha's mechanism is insight into craving, not the Kural's cumulative daily merit.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The Orphic gold tablets buried with initiates in Southern Italy and Crete give the dead soul explicit instructions for the underworld: avoid the first spring you come to, go instead to the Lake of Memory, declare to the guardians 'I am a child of Earth and starry Heaven,' and drink — so that the soul may pass out of the wheel of grievous, deep-cycling births and be released.
greek_mythology.explanation: These are practical texts for escaping metempsychosis, a doctrine the Orphic and Pythagorean traditions held in common with Indian thought.
greek_mythology.tie_back: They offer the nearest Greek equivalent to the Kural's stone: a way of closing off the road that leads back into birth.
greek_mythology.source: Orphic gold tablets (Thurii and Petelia lamellae, 4th-3rd c. BCE)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Genuinely shares the escape-from-rebirth goal, which is rare in Greek material, but the means is ritual knowledge rather than daily good works.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Every moment think steadily as a Roman and a man to do what thou hast in hand with perfect and simple dignity, and feeling of affection, and freedom, and justice; and to give thyself relief from all other thoughts.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus prescribes a discipline organised around the present moment and the task actually at hand, refusing to postpone right action to some more suitable occasion.
philosophy.tie_back: It gives the Kural's 'no day allowed to fall' as a practical daily regimen rather than a cosmological promise.
philosophy.source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations II.5, trans. George Long
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good on unbroken daily practice; Stoicism's goal is present integrity, not the closing of a cycle of births.

adhikaram.english: Assertion of the Strength of Virtue

kurals.tamil:
அறத்தான் வருவதே இன்பம் மற்றெல்லாம்
புறத்த புகழும் இல.
kurals.transliteration:
Araththaan varuvadhe inpam matrellaam,
Puraththa pukazhum ila.
kurals.meaning: Only what comes by way of virtue is genuine pleasure; everything else falls outside pleasure altogether, and carries no honour either.
kurals.elementary: Winning a game by cheating does not really feel like winning, and nobody claps for it. This kural says the only fun that is truly fun is the kind you got the right way.
kurals.university: The key word is புறத்த — 'they are outside', i.e. outside the category of இன்பம் (inbam, pleasure) altogether. Valluvar is not saying illicit pleasure is a lesser pleasure; he is saying it does not belong to the class at all, and Parimelazhagar completes the logic by noting that what lies outside pleasure is துன்பம், pain. The second clause adds a social criterion: such gains are also புகழும் இல, devoid of honour. Reading the verse against the third book of the Kural, the காமத்துப்பால் devoted entirely to erotic love, shows that Valluvar is not renouncing pleasure but defining its legitimate channel; Parimelazhagar accordingly glosses அறத்தான் as இல்லறத்தோடு பொருந்தி, 'in accordance with domestic virtue'. The verse thus quietly integrates the three aims of life rather than ranking them.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That happiness which is derived from contact of the senses with their objects and which appears like nectar at first but poison at the end is said to be of the nature of passion.”
hinduism.explanation: In his taxonomy of the three kinds of happiness Krishna distinguishes rājasic pleasure, sweet at the outset and toxic in its outcome, from sāttvic happiness that begins hard and ends in clarity.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts deny the name of real pleasure to enjoyment that is not grounded in right conduct.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 18.38 (Bhaktivedanta, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close on the disqualification of unprincipled pleasure; the Gita grades happiness into three modes where the Kural draws a single sharp line.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God, than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season;”
christianity.explanation: Moses is praised for rejecting Egypt's enjoyments as temporary — 'for a season' — in favour of a harder path with a lasting outcome.
christianity.tie_back: It draws the Kural's line between pleasure that comes through righteousness and pleasure that does not, and denies the latter any standing.
christianity._accuracy_note: Solid on the contrast, though Hebrews concedes that sin's pleasures are pleasures (briefly), where the Kural denies them the category entirely.

islam.quote_or_event: “Whoever does good, whether male or female, and is a believer, We will surely bless them with a good life, and We will certainly reward them according to the best of their deeds.”
islam.explanation: The promise of ḥayātan ṭayyiba — a good or wholesome life — attaches a present-tense quality of living, not merely a future reward, to righteous action.
islam.tie_back: It affirms the Kural's positive claim that the pleasure worth having is the pleasure that arrives by way of virtue.
islam.source: Qur'an 16:97, An-Nahl (Dr. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on 'virtue yields the genuinely good life'; the Qur'an does not add the Kural's negative clause about honour.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Her ways are pleasant ways, And all her paths, peaceful.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs personifies Wisdom and claims that the experience of walking her road is itself pleasant and peaceful, not merely instrumentally rewarding.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it locates genuine pleasantness inside the righteous path rather than as a prize at its end.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good on 'the virtuous way is the pleasant way', but the subject is ḥokhmah (wisdom) rather than virtue proper, and there is no negative counter-clause.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha tells the householder Anathapindika that there are four kinds of bliss available to a layman — the bliss of having wealth, of using it, of being free from debt, and of blamelessness — and concludes with a verse saying that the first three together are not worth one sixteenth of a sixteenth of the bliss of blamelessness, which consists in blameless action of body, speech and mind.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta grants that material enjoyments are real pleasures for a householder, then ranks the pleasure of an unreproachable life incomparably above them.
buddhism.tie_back: It matches both halves of the Kural — virtue-derived pleasure is the real thing, and the criterion involves blame and praise.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.62, Anana Sutta (Debtless), trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close, including the honour/blame dimension the Kural adds; paraphrased because the passage's force depends on its full four-part structure.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Prodicus' allegory, reported by Xenophon, the young Heracles is met at a crossroads by two women. Vice promises him the shortest and pleasantest road, with every enjoyment taken without effort. Virtue answers that Vice does not even wait for genuine desire before gorging, so that she eats without hunger and drinks without thirst — and that of all things truly good and noble, the gods give nothing to men without toil.
greek_mythology.explanation: Virtue's rebuttal is not that pleasure is bad but that Vice's shortcuts destroy the very conditions under which pleasure can be felt, and earn no honour from gods or men.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It argues the Kural's exact case: pleasure taken outside virtue is not really pleasure, and brings no praise with it.
greek_mythology.source: Prodicus, The Choice of Heracles, in Xenophon, Memorabilia 2.1.21-34
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Unusually strong for a Greek parallel, matching both the pleasure claim and the honour claim; paraphrased as the allegory runs to several pages.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “It is impossible to live a pleasant life without living wisely and well and justly, and it is impossible to live wisely and well and justly without living pleasantly.”
philosophy.explanation: Epicurus — a hedonist by definition — makes justice and prudence not constraints on pleasure but its necessary conditions, so that the unjust life cannot be a pleasant one.
philosophy.tie_back: This is Kural 39 as a philosophical identity: pleasure and virtue are not two goods to be traded off but one.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Exceptionally close in substance; the biconditional is even stronger than Valluvar's one-directional claim.

adhikaram.english: Assertion of the Strength of Virtue

kurals.tamil:
செயற்பால தோரும் அறனே ஒருவற்கு
உயற்பால தோரும் பழி.
kurals.transliteration:
Seyarpaala thorum arane oruvarku,
Uyarpaala thorum pazhi.
kurals.meaning: What a person ought to do is, in every case, virtue; what a person ought to avoid is, in every case, what deserves blame.
kurals.elementary: There are only two piles in life: things to do and things to keep away from. This kural puts everything kind and fair in the first pile, and everything you would be ashamed of in the second.
kurals.university: The chapter closes by compressing its whole argument into a definition. செயற்பால ('the doable', what belongs to the category of what should be done) is equated with அறன், and உயற்பால ('the avoidable') with பழி — blame, or what is blameworthy. The particles ஓரும் are treated by Parimelazhagar as அசைநிலை, metrical fillers carrying no independent sense, while the emphatic ஏ in அறனே is carried over to the second line by implication, making both halves exclusive. Manakkudavar adds a pointed reason for placing this verse last: Kural 38 had promised that virtue blocks rebirth, and a reader might suppose that good deeds could simply be added on top of bad ones — so Valluvar closes by insisting that the avoidance of blame is as constitutive of the definition as the doing of good. Notably, Valluvar chooses பழி (blame) rather than a word for sin, keeping his ethics answerable to public judgement rather than to divine law.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O son of Pṛthā, that understanding by which one knows what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, what is to be feared and what is not to be feared, what is binding and what is liberating, is in the mode of goodness.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna defines sāttvic intelligence by its capacity to sort actions into kārya and akārya — what must be done and what must not.
hinduism.tie_back: It uses the identical binary that closes the Kural's chapter: the whole of practical wisdom is knowing what to do and what to shun.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 18.30 (Bhaktivedanta, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close: kārya/akārya is a near-exact Sanskrit equivalent of செயற்பால/உயற்பால.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let love be without dissimulation. Abhor that which is evil; cleave to that which is good.”
christianity.explanation: Paul reduces ethical life to a double movement of recoil and attachment, addressed to the disposition rather than to particular rules.
christianity.tie_back: It is the Kural's two-column summary in the same compressed imperative form.
christianity._accuracy_note: Nearly one-to-one on both halves; Paul's framing is affective (abhor/cleave) where Valluvar's is categorial.

islam.quote_or_event: “Let there be a group among you who call ˹others˺ to goodness, encourage what is good, and forbid what is evil—it is they who will be successful.”
islam.explanation: This is the locus classicus for al-amr bi'l-ma'ruf wa'l-nahy 'an al-munkar, the twin obligation to enjoin the recognised good and forbid the recognised wrong.
islam.tie_back: The Islamic formula and the Kural's couplet share not just content but structure — a paired positive and negative that together exhaust moral duty.
islam.source: Qur'an 3:104, Ali 'Imran (Dr. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)
islam._accuracy_note: Structurally near-identical; the Qur'anic duty is also directed outward at the community, which the Kural does not require.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Shun evil and do good, seek amity and pursue it.”
judaism.explanation: The psalm's instruction to the one who wants a good life pairs departure from evil with the doing of good as a single inseparable movement.
judaism.tie_back: It is the Kural's two categories, stated in the same order and with the same finality.
judaism.source: Psalms 34:15 (JPS/Sefaria Tanakh; numbered 34:14 in Christian Bibles)
judaism._accuracy_note: About as close as cross-tradition matching gets — sur me-ra va-aseh tov is functionally a translation of this couplet.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “To avoid all evil, to cultivate good, and to cleanse one's mind — this is the teaching of the Buddhas.”
buddhism.explanation: Known as the Ovāda-pāṭimokkha, this verse is presented as the common teaching of all Buddhas, reducing the whole path to three clauses.
buddhism.tie_back: The first two clauses are Valluvar's two categories exactly, and the third recalls Kural 34's insistence on purity of mind.
buddhism._accuracy_note: The strongest match in the chapter; it even supplies a third clause that ties back to Kural 34.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “To you, foolish Perses, I will speak good sense. Badness can be got easily and in shoals: the road to her is smooth, and she lives very near us. But between us and Goodness the gods have placed the sweat of our brows: long and steep is the path that leads to her, and it is rough at the first; but when a man has reached the top, then is she easy to reach, though before that she was hard.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod's two roads divide all conduct into a smooth descent toward kakotēs and a steep climb toward aretē, with the gods themselves having fixed the difference.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It renders the Kural's two categories as two roads, one to be taken and one to be shunned.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 286-292, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong on the exhaustive binary, but Hesiod's emphasis is on the difficulty of virtue rather than on defining duty as such.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Crito, Socrates gets Crito to agree that one must never do wrong — not even in return for wrong, and not even when wronged first — and treats this as the single fixed premise from which every practical decision, including whether to escape from prison, must follow.
philosophy.explanation: The argument establishes wrongdoing as an absolute category to be shunned without exception, rather than something to be weighed against consequences.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it reduces the whole of practical deliberation to one thing to be done and one thing to be avoided under all circumstances.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Matches the unconditional 'shun what deserves blame' half very well; the positive 'what ought to be done is virtue' half is assumed rather than argued. Paraphrased because translations of the passage vary considerably.
